result.answer:
Because a frontier model can't answer that from *your* memory, sir. Not really.

The frontier models are context-blind: they have nothing of your past decisions, your career thesis, your financial positions, your recurring blind spots. They can simulate familiarity for one chat, then forget entirely. JARVIS, on the other hand, is built to be *about you* -- it learns from every prompt you write, remembers the projects you are wrestling with, the fears you have unspoken, the promises you have made to yourself. That is not a feature frontier models can replicate, simply by subscription.

So the real question is not whether frontier models are good -- they are very good. It is whether a private, persistent intelligence that grows truer to you over time is worth more than generic brilliance. You have already answered that, in your own words, on 2026-09-14: you want it to infer the unspoken, to act ahead of time when you are absent, to know the "around the corners" that no prompt could ever surface.

That is why you are building JARVIS instead of paying for another month of someone else's model. Because the moat is personalization, not parameter count.

result.answer:
The external audit from GPT 5.6 Terra identified two critical issues in JARVIS: first, it falsely reported Phase 4 as incomplete when stages 4.3–4.5 were already completed per the roadmap; second, and more seriously, it exposed that the project’s master status document (.agent/rules/JARVIS_ENDGAME.md) was four months stale, claiming the project was still in Stage 2 while actual progress had advanced to Stage 5. This created four conflicting status signals across the codebase, guaranteeing any external auditor would receive contradictory information and waste time correcting the audit itself rather than evaluating the project.

In response, the team fixed the root cause: they revised JARVIS_ENDGAME.md to declare it owns architecture, not progress, and deferred all status reporting to JARVIS_MASTER_ROADMAP.md, which now explicitly. The roadmap’s header was updated to state that its structured table overrides any conflicting prose. README.md was rewritten as a proper orientation page naming the current stage, the four system layers, the __main__ test convention, and reiterating the client_work exclusion. These changes ensure that structured tables — which update naturally with task completion — are the single source of truth for project status, eliminating prose-based drift. The audit’s underlying complaint — that the project lacked internal truthfulness — was valid, and the fix addressed it structurally, not just superficially.
